summary: Redwood AE/SE ran a lab-style walkthrough of the Console's request forensics, tracing, and error analysis features. Conversation focused on how to map request paths, identify root causes (model fallback, KV cache misses, routing), secure data in transit for VPC/private deployments, and scope a 2-week POC to reproduce a high-severity production error. Customer asked detailed SSO/KMS/KV cache questions and requested runbook examples and a small benchmark/trace set to validate behavior.
topics: KV cache misses and prefix caching
SLOs and latency vs cost tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Gupta (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Rios (Veridian), Jonas Lee (Veridian CTO), Priya Menon (SRE), Sam Ortiz (Product), Lina Zhao (Data Privacy)

[00:00] Ethan Morales: hey everyone, thanks for making time, i'm ethan from redwood inference, and with me is priya our solutions engineer. we wanted to run a hands-on lab, um, to go through request-level forensics in the console — the trace maps, request logs, and how we typically debug root cause across fallbacks and kv cache behavior.
[00:18] Jonas Lee: thanks, ethan. high level, we had a sev last week where outputs went stale then we saw a spike in token cost. so main things: why did fallback trigger, where did latency come from, and how to avoid in future.
[00:35] Priya Gupta: yep, that's perfect. we'll start with a quick demo of a request timeline — the hop map — then we'll pull a couple of example traces that show a model fallback, a kv cache miss, and an infra retry. i'll also show how to link to the raw request logs and the model-side metrics.
[00:50] Dr. Maya Rios: quick one, is this the hosted console or our private deployment? our security team will want to understand what telemetry leaves the VPC.
[00:58] Ethan Morales: good call. for the demo we'll use a sandbox tenant on hosted, but all the artifacts and the features are the same for Dedicated and Private; we'll call out what changes for VPC / private control plane.
[01:12] Priya Gupta: starting screen share now — ok, here's the request list, you can see filters on model, route, status. i'm going to pick a failed request from last week — see this one flagged with high token spend and an error code 504-ish.
[01:30] [01:30] Priya Gupta: the trace timeline — we show time per stage: routing -> model call -> kv cache lookup -> response assembly. you can expand the model call to see kernel-level timings, queue time, and the selected execution variant, e.g., quantized vs fp16.
[01:47] Sam Ortiz: when you say 'kv cache' is that the prefix cache? or is it the per-request kv? we have a large prompt prefix, and sometimes we'd prefer cache hits.
[01:58] Priya Gupta: it's both — prefix cache is our automatic prefix/KV caching: if we detect repeating prefixes we cache KV pages. there's also explicit per-request KV cache control via the SDK headers. we surface the hit/miss at the trace level.
[02:14] Priya Menon: can you show an example of a miss leading to longer model time? that's what we saw — long tail on a subset of requests.
[02:21] Priya Gupta: sure, zooming in — here's a trace with a miss: you can see the kv lookup returned cold, which pushed more context to the model and the kernel selection jumped to a longer-path execution; see the extra 200–350 ms there, and token spend went up because more decoding happened.
[02:40] [02:40] Dr. Maya Rios: i notice the model fallback in the trace, it tried a smaller variant first?
[02:47] Priya Gupta: in this tenant the routing policy is cost-prefer then latency-fallback. so it tried a cheaper quantized variant, but because of the longer context it timed out and the router retried to a larger fp16 model. that retry doubled the per-request cost.
[03:05] Jonas Lee: is there a way to set a hard SLO that avoids retries? we sometimes prefer a fast, slightly lower quality answer over paying double.
[03:13] Priya Gupta: yes — in routing policies you can set max retry budget and fallback behavior: either prefer cheaper models with best-effort, or fail fast to a configured error code. also you can pin a model variant per route to avoid any fallback.
[03:31] Ethan Morales: quick commercial note — Dedicated capacity gives you more predictable throughput so you see fewer kernel hops and retries under load; for cost-sensitive flows many customers run a small dedicated pool for critical routes.
[03:45] Lina Zhao: on data privacy — if we do Dedicated or Private, does telemetry like request text and traces remain in our VPC?
[03:52] Ethan Morales: with Private deployments the control plane is customer-managed and telemetry can be routed to your internal logging — you can choose to redact request text at ingest or only store metadata. for Hosted we (Redwood) retain traces per the retention policy but we offer field-level redaction and bring-your-own-kms for encrypting at rest.
[04:15] [04:15] Priya Gupta: back to the trace — here's a combined view with the console's error correlation: we show error clusters (timeouts, model OOM, kv miss) and you can click to see all requests in that cluster and to export a CSV for downstream triage.
[04:31] Sam Ortiz: how accurate is the clustering? we've seen noise in automated clusters before.
[04:36] Priya Gupta: clustering is heuristic-based and you can supply custom rules — e.g., cluster by substring in stack, by error code range, or by top-of-stack fingerprint. we also support manual labeling and you can feed labels back into the quality monitor.
[04:51] [05:00] Ethan Morales: let's walk through a root-cause hypothesis: the sev looked like token burn + stale outputs. hypothesis one: prefix cache miss combined with quantized variant timeout caused retry; hypothesis two: upstream client sent duplicate requests causing double billing; hypothesis three: model regression in that version increased decode steps. we'll show how to validate each with traces and logs.
[05:24] [05:24] Priya Gupta: validating the cache miss: filter traces by kv_hit=false and by route. here's the histogram of request latencies for kv_hit vs kv_miss — you can see the 95th jumps.
[05:36] Dr. Maya Rios: can we integrate these traces with our existing SRE pager system? we want alerts when key patterns appear.
[05:42] Priya Gupta: yes, you can export alerts via webhook or forward anomalies into your monitoring (PagerDuty, Datadog). console has an alert rule builder: example rule - > if cluster 'kv_miss' > 3% for 5m -> fire webhook.
[06:00] [06:00] Jonas Lee: network question: with Private, do we require VPC peering or is it egress? we have strict egress rules.
[06:08] Ethan Morales: for Private you run a control plane in your VPC; data plane stays in your environment. we support IP allowlist, VPC peering, and egress narrows; we'll share the network diagram. for hosted, we support VPC peering and customer-provided NAT for egress control.
[06:30] Priya Menon: what about key management? we need to use our HSM, not Redwood KMS.
[06:36] Priya Gupta: BYOK (bring your own key) is supported for Private and Dedicated via integrations with major KMS/HSM offerings; we can show the config snippet.
[06:46] [07:00] Priya Gupta: next demo - request playback: you can replay a historical request into a sandbox model and see how different model variants respond, plus measure token delta and latency. i'm going to replay the failing request into two variants.
[07:15] [07:15] Priya Gupta: replay 1 -> quantized v1: it times out at ~1.2s; replay 2 -> fp16 v2: completes in 0.6s but costs 2x tokens. console shows per-token breakdown.
[07:30] Sam Ortiz: can we automate replay against a set of golden requests nightly?
[07:35] Priya Gupta: yes — we have a replay API and scheduled jobs; many customers run nightly replays against canary model variants to detect regressions.
[07:46] [08:00] Dr. Maya Rios: about retention — how long do traces live? our privacy policy is strict.
[08:06] Ethan Morales: retention is configurable per-tenant; default 30 days for hosted, but you can increase or decrease and set redaction rules. for Private you control retention entirely.
[08:20] Priya Gupta: moving on, here's the request inspector which shows the raw request payload, request headers (we obfuscate tokens), and the model prompt slice. note sometimes the transcription will show 'speaker 6' because of upload metadata, that's normal.
[08:40] [08:40] Jonas Lee: we also saw an unusual pattern where a batch of requests had identical client request-ids but different IPs — could that be a client-side retry?
[08:50] Priya Gupta: identical request-id with different client IP usually means client retried without dedup; our logs show dedup keys and time windows. you can set idempotency windows per-route to avoid double billing.
[09:05] [09:05] Priya Gupta: switching to the error waterfall view — this shows the order errors occurred in the trace chain; you can annotate and then jump to the request in raw logs. you can also attach a runbook link to a cluster so responders see the recommended triage steps.
[09:22] Sam Ortiz: would love a starter runbook we can adapt.
[09:25] Priya Gupta: absolutely — i'll attach our 'request-failure-runbook' template to the follow-up.
[09:33] [09:33] Ethan Morales: quick question for the privacy/regs team — Lina, do you have constraints about storing PII inside traces?
[09:40] Lina Zhao: we avoid storing raw user text unless necessary; if we must, it needs to be encrypted with our key and retained under 90 days and be auditable. also need SOC2 evidence.
[09:51] Ethan Morales: that's fine — we'll mark those fields as redacted by default and we'll include the SOC2 docs in the package.
[10:00] [10:00] Priya Gupta: jumping to live demo of lazy prefix caching: here's a time series showing savings after enabling lazy caching on a route — token cost per request drops as hits increase. you can configure cache TTL and eviction.
[10:22] Dr. Maya Rios: is eviction LRU?
[10:25] Priya Gupta: default is LRU with size caps, but you can plug in policy hints based on route.
[10:32] [11:00] Priya Gupta: now the tracing internals: each request gets a unique trace id, we correlate to model-side logs, execution kernel metrics, and infra metrics. these are stitched server-side; sometimes model names are fuzzy in transcript exports because of auto-ocr or tokenization differences.
[11:19] Jonas Lee: what about correlating with our internal request-id? we have a global X-Request-ID.
[11:24] Priya Gupta: pass your X-Request-ID in the header and we'll surface it in traces; you can also attach annotations. we commonly see customers do this for end-to-end debugging.
[11:36] [12:00] Ethan Morales: let's talk scale: under burst load, retries and fallback behavior are often the biggest cost driver. we recommend either pinning for critical routes or ensuring your reserved capacity covers peak load to avoid router fallback loops.
[12:18] Priya Menon: for the POC, we'll probably want to simulate our peak daily patterns rather than a constant qps. can you accept trace replays with time-shifted intervals?
[12:26] Priya Gupta: yes, replay API supports time-shift and variable arrival distributions. we'll include the harness.
[12:34] [13:00] Priya Gupta: demoing audit logs: here's the per-tenant audit trail for config changes, routing policy updates, and model pinning — logs are tamper-evident and can be exported to your SIEM.
[13:22] Lina Zhao: SIEM integration is mandatory. which log formats do you support?
[13:27] Priya Gupta: we support syslog, JSON over HTTPS, and cloud storage sinks (S3/GCS).
[13:35] [14:00] Ethan Morales: quick pause — any red flags from your side so far?
[14:05] Dr. Maya Rios: just the items around BYOK and retention which you addressed. also we'd want to confirm the SLA around trace retention for compliance.
[14:15] Ethan Morales: we'll include SLA language in the follow-up.
[14:21] [14:30] Priya Gupta: bringing up the test harness: here are the sample traces we recommend sending — 50 failing requests, 100 normal, and a burst scenario. we'll run them through the replay and compare quantized vs fp16 and show cost deltas.
[14:45] Sam Ortiz: for the POC success criteria, propose: reproduce the failure, show 10–20% cost improvement with caching/pinning, and demonstrate alerting tied to our PagerDuty.
[14:58] Ethan Morales: good, that'll be in the POC doc.
[15:05] [15:00] Priya Gupta: one more advanced view — the console exposes a model internals pane: token-level attention heatmaps and kernel switching events. helpful to understand when kernel choices inflate latency.
[15:21] Jonas Lee: kernel switching — is that visible only for open models or also for some third-party runtimes?
[15:26] Priya Gupta: depends on the runtime telemetry; for our curated models we surface it. for 3rd party closed models we show timing but not kernel internals.
[15:39] [16:00] Priya Gupta: there's a question in chat about cost attribution — console breaks down cost by tokenization, decoding, and model selection so you can trace cost spikes to a specific stage.
[16:08] Dr. Maya Rios: can we create a dashboard of top cost drivers?
[16:12] Priya Gupta: yes — custom dashboards with per-route cost and top offending requests.
[16:20] [17:00] Ethan Morales: now the bit about automated fallbacks and guardrails — we can attach a policy that if a retry would push cost above X or latency above Y, then don't retry and instead return a fast error code. this reduces user-visible flakiness and unbounded cost loops.
[17:23] Priya Menon: we'd rather fail fast for some user-facing flows.
[17:27] Priya Gupta: you can set route-level guardrails for that.
[17:36] [18:00] Priya Gupta: let's also show correlation with model quality logs — if the quality monitor sees regressions tied to a model version, it creates an annotation on traces so ops sees both quality and infra signals.
[18:16] Sam Ortiz: that helps when product sees answer drift.
[18:20] [19:00] Priya Gupta: jumping ahead: the playback can also simulate a hybrid routing policy where for specific keys you always route to dedicated capacity; very useful for VIP users.
[19:11] Jonas Lee: question — licensing for Dedicated: do we get reserved GPUs or is it soft reservation?
[19:18] Ethan Morales: Dedicated is reserved capacity; we offer commit tiers. we'll send a pricing sheet but typical customers commit to a baseline and have burst.
[19:31] [20:00] Dr. Maya Rios: are we able to run this POC with data residency in eu-west? we have eu users and regs.
[20:09] Ethan Morales: yes we have regional deployments; we'll confirm region availability for the POC and note any lead time for Dedicated in a given region.
[20:20] [21:00] Priya Gupta: moving to the final section — recommended runbook steps when you see this kind of trace: 1) identify cluster (kv_miss / fallback), 2) check replay behavior, 3) examine dedup headers / client request-id, 4) if retry loop, change routing policy to fail fast and pin model, 5) enable lazy prefetch or increase cache TTL. we'll attach a template.
[21:34] Dr. Maya Rios: can you send the runbook as markdown? our SREs will adopt it.
[21:40] Priya Gupta: yes — markdown and Confluence-ready copy.
[21:46] [22:00] Ethan Morales: wrapping to logistics — we'll share: SOC2/ISO packet, sample traces, replay harness, pricing for Dedicated and hosted, and a proposed POC schedule. any additional asks?
[22:12] Lina Zhao: include the SIEM format and an example redaction policy.
[22:18] Ethan Morales: noted.
[22:24] [23:00] Priya Gupta: last quick tip — enabling request-level idempotency and client-side dedup dramatically reduces double billing; if you can't change client, we can set idempotency windows server-side.
[23:38] Jonas Lee: good to know.
[23:42] [24:00] Sam Ortiz: let's capture success criteria: reproduce failure, reduce cost by at least 10% via caching/pinning or routing, and demonstrate PagerDuty alerting.
[24:12] Ethan Morales: perfect, we'll reflect that in the POC doc.
[24:20] [25:00] Dr. Maya Rios: one more compliance note — will you give evidence of key rotation procedures?
[25:08] Ethan Morales: yes, in the security packet. for BYOK we'll show rotation steps and attestations.
[25:18] [26:00] Priya Gupta: closing the demo — now moving to Q&A and next logistical steps.
[26:12] Jonas Lee: ok, timeline-wise we want a kickoff the week of may 5, two-week scope, with an interim check after week 1.
[26:22] Ethan Morales: sounds doable. we'll propose May 5 start.
[26:28] [27:00] Dr. Maya Rios: for the sample traces, what's the preferred format?
[27:05] Priya Gupta: newline-delimited JSON with trace-id, request-id, timestamp, payload hash; we'll send a template.
[27:14] Priya Menon: would love if the sample includes a couple of replay scripts.
[27:18] Priya Gupta: included.
[27:23] [28:00] Ethan Morales: final recap: we'll send security docs, runbook, sample traces, a pricing sketch, and POC calendar. action items in chat. thanks everyone.
[28:38] Dr. Maya Rios: thanks, ethan, priya. helpful lab.
[28:42] Jonas Lee: appreciate it. we'll follow up with network diagrams.
[28:47] [end]

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker numbering and minor mis-hearings present (e.g., 'kv cache' spelled various ways), timestamps approximate.
